lessons.title: Fire safety: fire triangle, classes of fire and extinguishers
lessons.summary: Fire questions are reliable marks: learn the fire triangle, the classes of fire, which extinguisher suits which class, and a handful of numbers on flash points and detection.

sections.h: The fire triangle and the fourth side
sections.html:
Stephen Court, Park Street

The Stephen Court fire on Park Street, Kolkata, in March 2010 started in an electrical fault and spread up a building with blocked exits and no working hydrants. Forty-three people died. Nearly every rule of fire safety was broken that day.

Every fire needs three things at the same time. This is the fire triangle.

SideWhat it means
Fuelsomething that burns
Oxygenusually from the air
Heatenough to start and keep the burning going

Remove any one side and the fire dies. The fire tetrahedron (a four-sided shape) adds a fourth side: the chain reaction. Inside a flame, tiny reactive bits called free radicals keep the burning going, one reaction setting off the next. Dry chemical powders and halons (older fire-fighting gases) work by breaking this chain.

Remember for the exam

Triangle: fuel, oxygen, heat. Tetrahedron adds the chain reaction.

The fourth element added in the fire tetrahedron is the:

  1. moisture
  2. fuel
  3. chain reaction
The fire triangle (and the 4th side)
Remove heat → cooling (water)
Remove oxygen → smothering (foam, CO₂, blanket)
Remove fuel → starving (shut valve, clear material)
Break the chain → dry powder, clean agents (the 4th side: tetrahedron)

sections.h: Four ways to put out a fire
sections.html:
Think of a kitchen. You turn off the gas knob, you put a lid on a burning pan, or you pour water on burning paper. Each one knocks out one side of the fire.

MethodWhat you removeHow
Starvingfueltake the fuel away
Smotheringoxygenfoam, CO₂, a fire blanket
Coolingheatwater
Breaking the chainchain reactionpowders, clean agents

Smothering means covering the fire so air cannot reach it. Clean agents are gases that put out fire without leaving residue.

Remember for the exam

Starve (fuel), smother (oxygen), cool (heat), break the chain (powders). Powders work mainly by breaking the chain reaction.

A fire blanket thrown over a burning pan puts the fire out by:

  1. smothering (cutting off oxygen)
  2. cooling
  3. starving
Four ways to put out a fire
1StarveRemove fuel
2SmotherCut oxygen: foam, CO₂
3CoolRemove heat: water
4Break the chainDry powder, clean agents

A godown in a Kolkata market can hold paper, paint, an LPG cylinder and cooking oil. Each burns differently, so fires are sorted into classes (Indian standard IS 2190 / IS 15683).

ClassFuelUseAvoid
Aordinary solids: wood, paper, clothwater, foam, ABC powder—
Bflammable liquids: petrol, oil, paintfoam, CO₂, dry powderwater jet
Cflammable gases: LPG, acetylenedry powder; shut off the gas—
Dmetals: magnesium, sodiumspecial dry powder, dry sandwater
F (US: K)cooking oils and fatswet chemicalwater
Electricallive equipment (not a separate class in IS)CO₂, dry powder; isolate supplywater, foam
Memory trick

A = Ash (solids that leave ash), B = Barrel (liquids), C = Cylinder (gases), D = Dense metals, F = Fat (cooking oil; the US calls it K). Water is safe only on A. IS 2190 itself defines A–D; the cooking-oil class appears in BIS guidance as F.

Remember for the exam

Petrol is Class B; metals are Class D. Never use water on oil, metal or live electrical fires.

Which extinguisher should be used on a live electrical panel fire?

  1. CO₂
  2. mechanical foam
  3. water
Classes of fire
AAsh: solidsWater, foam, ABC powder
BBarrel: liquidsFoam, CO₂, powder; no water jet
CCylinder: gasesPowder; shut off the gas
DDense metalsSpecial powder, dry sand
FFat: cooking oil (US: K)Wet chemical

On a factory inspection you will see extinguishers on the walls. Each type suits certain classes.

TypeClassesNotes
Water (gas pressure / stored pressure)A only—
Mechanical foam (AFFF)A and Bforms a blanket on burning liquids
CO₂B and electricalcools and smothers
Dry chemical powder (DCP)BC or ABCBC uses sodium bicarbonate; ABC uses mono-ammonium phosphate, the most versatile
Clean agentsserver rooms, control roomsreplacing halon, an ozone depleter

More on the CO₂ extinguisher:

  • Red body (Indian standard IS 15683; the black band is a UK convention).
  • It has a discharge horn (the nozzle), non-metallic for live electrical equipment.
  • Not for confined spaces: the gas can cause asphyxiation (suffocation).
Remember for the exam

Water: A only. Foam: A and B. CO₂: B and electrical. ABC powder = mono-ammonium phosphate.

ABC dry powder extinguishers contain:

  1. mono-ammonium phosphate
  2. sodium bicarbonate
  3. carbon dioxide

In a fire drill at a jute mill, workers are taught four words for using any portable extinguisher: PASS.

LetterAction
PPull the pin
AAim at the base of the flames
SSqueeze the handle
SSweep side to side

The fuel is at the base, so that is where the agent must go. Spraying into the flames above wastes it.

Examiner's twist

Aim at the base of the flames, not the flames themselves. And a CO₂ extinguisher's horn gets extremely cold; hold it by the handle. Both points appear as "which is correct" options.

Remember for the exam

PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.

In PASS, the "A" stands for:

  1. activate
  2. aim at the base of the fire
  3. alarm

Look up at the ceiling of a big Kolkata mall and you may see small glass bulbs. These are sprinklers, part of the building's fixed fire systems (built in, not carried by hand).

SystemWhat it does
Sprinklera glass bulb bursts at a set temperature and releases water; red bulb 68 °C is most common
Hydranta water outlet for fire hoses
Deluge systemsprays water through many open heads at once
Smoke detectorionisation or optical type
Heat detectorsenses a rise in temperature
Manual call pointan alarm point a person operates by hand
Remember for the exam

The most common sprinkler bulb is red and bursts at 68 °C. Smoke detectors are ionisation or optical.

The most common sprinkler bulb colour and its bursting temperature are:

  1. blue, 23 °C
  2. red, 93 °C
  3. red, 68 °C

At a petrol pump you see "No smoking" boards everywhere, because petrol gives off vapour that can catch fire even on a cool day. Three temperatures describe this.

TermPlain meaning
Flash pointlowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to ignite momentarily
Fire pointa few degrees higher; the vapour keeps burning
Auto-ignition temperaturethe liquid ignites without a flame

The Petroleum Rules 2002 group petroleum by flash point:

ClassFlash pointExample
Class Abelow 23 °Cpetrol
Class B23–65 °Ckerosene, diesel
Class C65–93 °Cfurnace oil
Memory trick

23 – 65 – 93 for petroleum classes A, B, C. Petrol is A (most dangerous), diesel and kerosene are B, furnace oil is C.

Remember for the exam

Flash point is lower than fire point, which is lower than auto-ignition temperature. Petrol is Class A.

Under the Petroleum Rules 2002, diesel is in:

  1. Class B
  2. Class A
  3. Class C
Petroleum classes by flash point
< 23 °C23–65 °C65–93 °C≥ 93 °C
Class A: petrolClass B: diesel, keroseneClass C: furnace oilExcluded: lube oil

A gas burns only when it is mixed with air in the right amount. Too little gas and the mix is too lean; too much and it is too rich. The band in between is the flammable range. Its lower end is the LEL (lower explosive limit) and its upper end the UEL (upper explosive limit).

GasFlammable range (% in air)
Methane5–15%
Hydrogen4–75%
Acetylene2.5–82% (widest)

Where a leaked gas goes matters too.

GasWeight compared with airWhere it collects
LPGheavierfloor level, in drains
Natural gaslighterrises

That is why an LPG leak in a kitchen is most dangerous low down, near the floor.

Remember for the exam

Methane 5–15%. Acetylene has the widest range. LPG sinks; natural gas rises.

The gas with the widest flammable range in this lesson is:

  1. methane
  2. acetylene
  3. hydrogen
Flammable range (% in air)
< 55–15> 15
Too leanMethane burnsToo rich
Hydrogen 4–75%; acetylene 2.5–82% (widest).

An LPG tanker caught in a fire is one of the worst sights for a fire brigade. The liquid inside boils, the pressure rises and the tank can burst.

TermMeaning
BLEVEBoiling Liquid Expanding Vapour Explosion, when a pressurised LPG tank is heated by fire
Dust explosion pentagonfive things a dust explosion needs: fuel, oxygen, ignition, dispersion, confinement

Dispersion means the dust is spread out in the air as a cloud. Confinement means it is inside an enclosed space. These two extra sides turn the fire triangle into a pentagon (a five-sided shape).

Remember for the exam

BLEVE = Boiling Liquid Expanding Vapour Explosion. The dust pentagon adds dispersion and confinement.

The two extra elements in the dust explosion pentagon are:

  1. carbon and nitrogen
  2. moisture and pressure
  3. dispersion and confinement

• Fire triangle: fuel, oxygen, heat. The tetrahedron adds the chain reaction.
  • Classes: A solids, B liquids, C gases, D metals, F cooking oil (US: K).
  • Water only on Class A. Never on oil, metal or live electrical fires.
  • CO₂ for B and electrical; ABC powder (mono-ammonium phosphate) is the most versatile.
  • PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.
  • Sprinkler red bulb: 68 °C.
  • Petroleum classes split at 23, 65 and 93 °C; petrol is Class A.
  • Methane 5–15%; acetylene widest; LPG heavier than air.
Two "Class" systems

"Petrol is Class B" (classes of fire: it is a flammable liquid) and "petrol is Class A" (Petroleum Rules 2002: flash point below 23 °C) are both true. Read which system the question names.

facts: Class A / B / C / D / F
Solids / liquids / gases / metals / cooking oil (US: K)
Pull, aim at base, squeeze, sweep
traps: Never use water on oil, metal or live electrical fires.
Flash point is lower than fire point, which is lower than auto-ignition temperature.
Aim at the base of the fire, not the flames.
recap: Triangle: fuel, oxygen, heat; tetrahedron adds the chain reaction.
A-B-C-D-F: ash, barrel, cylinder, dense metal, fat (cooking oil; K in the US).

mcqs.q: A fire involving petrol is a:
mcqs.e: Petrol is a flammable liquid, and flammable liquids are Class B.

mcqs.q: Which agent is unsuitable for a Class B (oil) fire?
mcqs.e: A water jet splashes and spreads the burning oil.
D is for metals such as magnesium, sodium, potassium and titanium.

mcqs.q: The fourth element added in the fire tetrahedron is:
mcqs.e: The triangle's three sides plus the chain reaction that keeps the flame going.

mcqs.q: Dry chemical powder extinguishes fire mainly by:
mcqs.e: The powder stops the free radicals that keep the burning going.

o: aim at the base of the fire
mcqs.e: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep. Aim at the base, where the fuel is.

mcqs.q: Under the Petroleum Rules, petrol is classed as:
mcqs.e: Its flash point is below 23 °C, so it is Class A.

mcqs.q: The flammable range of methane in air is:
mcqs.e: Methane burns between 5% and 15% in air. 4–75% is hydrogen.

mcqs.q: LPG leaks are most dangerous at:
mcqs.e: LPG is heavier than air, so it sinks and collects low down.

mcqs.q: The lowest temperature at which a liquid gives off enough vapour to ignite momentarily is its:
mcqs.e: That is the flash point. The fire point is a little higher and keeps the burning going.
